title: FM, SSB and signal bandwidth
blurb: How AM, FM and SSB differ, how wide each signal is, and which to choose for repeaters, weak signals and sidebands.

T8A01.why: SSB is amplitude modulation with the carrier and one sideband removed, so it belongs to the **AM family**.
T8A01.trap: PSK and packet are digital methods, not amplitude modulation.

T8A02.why: VHF packet uses **FM or PM**: the signal varies frequency (or phase), not height.

T8A03.why: **SSB** is narrow and efficient, so it carries the weakest signals farthest on VHF/UHF.
T8A03.trap: FM is for local repeater work, not weak-signal DX.

T8A04.why: Repeaters use **FM or PM**. The signal changes frequency to carry the voice.

T8A05.why: **CW** is just a carrier switched on and off, about 150 Hz wide: far narrower than any voice or picture signal.

T8A06.why: At 10 MHz and above, including 10 m, VHF and UHF, convention is **upper sideband**.
T8A06.trap: Lower sideband is the convention below 10 MHz (80 and 40 m).

T8A07.why: SSB drops the carrier and one sideband, so it is **narrower** than FM.
T8A07.trap: SSB is harder to tune than FM, and no mode is immune to interference.

T8A08.why: A voice SSB signal is about **3 kHz** wide, roughly the range of the voice.

T8A09.why: FM voice on repeaters takes **10 to 15 kHz**, several times wider than SSB.

T8A10.why: Fast-scan TV carries a full moving picture and needs about **6 MHz**.
T8A10.trap: A voice-sized figure is far too small: a moving picture carries thousands of times more information.

T8A11.why: CW needs only about **150 Hz**, the narrowest of all common modes.
T8A11.trap: 2.4 kHz is SSB-like and 15 kHz is FM-like.

T8A12.why: On FM only **one signal is received at a time**: the stronger one wins the channel. SSB lets you hear a weaker signal under a stronger one.
T8A12.trap: FM voice quality is good, and FM is easier, not harder, to tune.
